title: 2 Kings 11:17–21
context: Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD, the king and the people that they will be the LORD’s people, and also between the king and the people. The people tear down the house of Baal and kill Mattan its priest. The guards and people escort the king to the palace, where he sits on the throne, and the city is quiet after Athaliah’s death. Versification: English 11:21 is Hebrew 12:1; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Both traditions read the covenant renewal as shared ground: restoring the Davidic king goes together with renewing the people’s loyalty to the LORD and removing the worship of Baal.

verses.text: Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, that they should be the LORD’s people; also between the king and the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD, the king and the people that they will be the LORD’s people, and also between the king and the people. The covenant is renewed.

Arminian readers note that the covenant calls for the people’s willing commitment to belong to the LORD, and that renewal of faith involves a conscious, communal choice to turn from false worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the covenant restores the proper order of Israel’s life: the king and people together under the LORD, reflecting God’s covenant purpose for his people and David’s line (2 Samuel 7:24).

Both traditions treat this verse as shared ground: true restoration means renewed loyalty to the LORD.

verses.text: All the people of the land went to the house of Baal, and broke it down. They broke his altars and his images in pieces thoroughly, and killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. The priest appointed officers over the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people tear down the house of Baal, smash its altars and images, and kill Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars; the priest appoints officers over the LORD’s house. False worship is removed.

Arminian readers note that the people act on their renewed commitment by removing the worship that had drawn them away, showing that repentance involves concrete change.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the destruction of Baal worship follows the covenant renewal, showing that God’s restoration of his people includes purifying their worship; the text reports Mattan’s death without elaboration.

Both traditions read the verse soberly as narrative of reform, without holding up the violence as a pattern for Christian practice.

verses.text: He took the captains over hundreds, and the Carites, and the guard, and all the people of the land; and they brought down the king from the LORD’s house, and came by the way of the gate of the guard to the king’s house. He sat on the throne of the kings.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada takes the commanders, the Carites, the guard and all the people, and they bring the king down from the LORD’s house to the palace by the gate of the guard, where he sits on the throne of the kings. The king takes his place.

Arminian readers note that the procession involves the whole community, showing broad support for the restoration.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king moves from the LORD’s house to the throne of the kings, a sequence that pictures royal authority flowing from God’s presence and covenant, and that David’s heir now sits on David’s throne as God had promised.

Both traditions see the enthronement as the fulfillment of God’s faithfulness to the house of David.

verses.text: So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. They had slain Athaliah with the sword at the king’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the people of the land rejoice, and the city is quiet, after Athaliah has been put to death with the sword at the king’s house. Peace returns.

Arminian readers note that the rejoicing of the people and the quiet of the city show the relief that comes when injustice is ended and rightful rule is restored, a blessing the whole community shares.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the quiet of the city reflects the peace that follows God’s restoration of rightful order, and that the narrative closes Athaliah’s story with a sober reminder of her end rather than celebration of violence.

Both traditions read the verse as the restoration of order and peace under God’s chosen king.

verses.text: Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash is seven years old when he begins to reign. In the Hebrew text this verse is 12:1, though the WEB numbers it 11:21.

Arminian readers note that the king’s youth makes him dependent on wise counsel, and that the coming chapter will show how much his early faithfulness owed to Jehoiada’s guidance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God placed a child on David’s throne, a reminder that the continuity of the dynasty rested on God’s faithfulness rather than on the strength or maturity of the king. The WEB spells his name both Jehoash and Joash in these chapters.

Both traditions read the verse as a transition to the account of his reign.
